mainEntity.name: How does Legendre’s formula count trailing zeros without multiplying everything?

acceptedAnswer.text: Each trailing zero needs one factor 10 = 2 × 5. Factors of 2 are more plentiful than 5s, so zeros equal the number of 5s in n!. Multiples of 5 contribute one each, multiples of 25 one more, multiples of 125 one more, and so on: Σ ⌊n/5ᵏ⌋.

mainEntity.name: What is the difference between Stirling’s formula and Ramanujan’s correction?

acceptedAnswer.text: Stirling’s leading term underestimates n! by roughly 1/(12n) in relative terms (0.83% at n = 10). Ramanujan’s version adds a cubic term under a sixth root, shrinking the relative error to about 9 × 10⁻⁸ at n = 10 (under 0.00001%).

mainEntity.name: How does this calculator avoid overflow?

acceptedAnswer.text: Ordinary 64-bit floating point overflows at 171! (about 10³⁰⁸). This page uses arbitrary-size integers for exact results up to 3,000!, and logarithms for the Stirling comparisons, so nothing overflows.

mainEntity.name: Is the double factorial (n!!) the factorial of a factorial?

acceptedAnswer.text: No. n!! multiplies every second number down from n (10!! = 10 · 8 · 6 · 4 · 2 = 3,840). The factorial of a factorial would be (n!)!, which is astronomically larger.

mainEntity.name: Can I take the factorial of a negative number or a fraction?

acceptedAnswer.text: Not with the whole-number definition. The Gamma function extends it to all real numbers except the negative integers, where it has poles: (−1)!, (−2)!, … are undefined. Use the Gamma tab for fractional values.
